name: RadixGates
question: Can a small Go gateway keep an SGLang pool serving when a node dies, and does its prefix routing still help on a real engine?
condition: clean completions in a node-crash test, against the original gateway (4 simulated workers, 16 clients, 30 s)
measured: Node-crash clean completions rose from 85.2% to 99.7% against the original, under the same injected faults; the test suite now has 55 tests.
judgment: On three real llama.cpp workers, the upgraded routing matched the original's cache hit rate (61.5% vs. 59.1%) rather than beating it, but cut the busiest worker's share of the prefill work from 73% to 43%.

name: lowbit-kernels
question: 4-bit projection weights move about 4× fewer bytes than FP16. On a Tesla T4, how much of that becomes decode speed, at what cost in quality, and where does it stop paying?
condition: CUDA-graph decode throughput of INT4 vs FP16, Qwen2.5-Instruct 0.5B–3B at batch 1 (Tesla T4); 3B peak memory 7.85 → 3.64 GB
measured: A GEMV ladder from one thread per row to multi-row warp tiling reached up to 75% of measured DRAM bandwidth; at batch 1 the deployed kernel takes 0.43–0.74× the time FP16 needs just to stream its weights. A tensor-core kernel and a dispatch rule from a 12-shape × 1–1,024-row sweep cover larger batches on one weight copy. Per-group clip search took 3B perplexity from 15.20 (absmax) to 10.83 (FP16 9.56); across the three models INT4 perplexity stays 13–39% above FP16.
judgment: Eager decode was 0.84–0.85× FP16 although the INT4 GPU work was shorter: host-side overhead set the pace, and CUDA Graph replay let the kernel gain show. Prefill still dequantizes to cuBLAS, so time to first token rises; against FP16 cuBLAS the INT4 path wins up to about 8–32 rows, depending on the layer.

name: llm-finetune-lab
question: Can a 0.5B model fine-tuned with LoRA answer questions about a database, on a laptop, without the data leaving it?
condition: of answers ran and returned the wrong rows (Q4_K_M, 391 held-out questions, scored by executing the SQL)
measured: Execution-correct answers rose from 42.7% to 82.6%; 16.4% ran cleanly but returned the wrong rows — invisible to a string-match check.
judgment: Guardrails only brought silent errors down to 9.1%, short of the 5% target, so the call was a human-reviewed suggestion tool, not an autonomous answerer.

name: cdc-chunker
question: How fast can content-defined chunking run in C++17 without changing where the chunks are?
condition: on 8 threads, chunks identical to the sequential chunker (256 MiB in memory, 8 KiB average chunk, Apple M1)
measured: About 2.0 GB/s on one thread, 7.4 GB/s on 8, output identical to sequential; 96.5% of a 67 MB source tree stayed reusable after 200 edits.
judgment: A merged LoRA model reused only 27.6% of its bytes against its base — ship the adapter, not the merged model.

name: FPGA matmul (HLS)
question: Can a 64×64 matrix multiply on the Ultra96's FPGA beat the Cortex-A53 on the same board, and how big must the problem be before offload pays?
condition: initiation interval at 150 MHz, from one result every 4 cycles to every cycle (64×64 FP32, C/RTL co-simulation passed)
measured: The stall was the memory read ports (2,048 bits/cycle needed); complete array partitioning reached II=1 in 320/360 DSPs and 49% BRAM. On the board: 0.496 ms per kernel vs 0.570 ms on the -O3 A53 (1.15×).
judgment: With 110 ms of OpenCL setup counted, break-even is N ≈ 395 and 10× needs N ≈ 1,112: offload only pays for larger or batched problems.

name: Cortex-A53 pipeline
question: How should a four-stage video pipeline be split across two A53 cores to get close to 2×?
condition: four-stage video pipeline, 53.2 → 97.4 frames/s, output bit-exact (Ultra96, two cores)
measured: Pipeline split at a point chosen from measured stage latency: 1.83×, vs 1.16× for row-split data parallelism (the compressor itself is sequential). A hand-written NEON kernel ran 1.34× over -O3 scalar.
judgment: Profiling on the target changed the plan: compression was 55% of x86 runtime, but on the A53 the filters and compression took 28–29% each, capping any single-stage speedup near 1.4×.

name: AVR input capture
question: When a timer overflow and an input capture arrive almost together, is the firmware's timestamp still right?
condition: wrong timestamps in 100 million random captures, for ISR latency under half a timer period (131 ms)
measured: A Timer1 input-capture ISR timestamps edges at 4 µs resolution; a 32-bit software count extends the 262 ms timer wrap; shared state is read through atomic snapshots.
judgment: Compiling the firmware logic for the host with the AVR's interrupt ordering made the race testable at scale; without the wrap rule, about 8% of captures were off by a full period.

name: conference-ops
question: When sixty people book the last ten seats at the same moment, and clients retry after timeouts, can a booking service stay exactly right?
condition: simultaneous registrations for 10 seats: exactly 10 confirmed, 50 waitlisted, counter equal to the rows (real PostgreSQL 16)
measured: 25 integration tests over real HTTP and PostgreSQL; with the row lock removed, the 60-request test fails, so it really detects the race.
judgment: Room and speaker double-booking is stopped by PostgreSQL exclusion constraints, not a check-then-insert in Java, which two requests at the same moment could slip past.

name: review-pipeline
question: How much does a careless train/test split flatter a model that predicts which reviews readers will find helpful?
condition: R² overstated by a random split (0.280) against a time split (0.061), 494K Amazon reviews, 97,798 held out
measured: Data contracts with line-numbered quarantine and idempotent, content-addressed stages; a clean run takes about 45 s and a rerun reproduces the same outputs.
judgment: The honest model is weak overall but useful where it counts: its top 10% of new reviews are helpful 50.0% of the time, 2.13× the 23.4% base rate.

name: budget-manager
question: When a bank's CSV has one bad row on line 4,000, can an import leave the ledger half written, and can restoring the wrong backup file destroy the real one?
condition: rows left in the ledger after importing a CSV that contains one bad row: the whole file is rejected (tested)
measured: 40 JUnit tests; line coverage is 97% in the domain layer and 92% in the services; a schema upgrade from V1 to V2 keeps existing rows, and a failing migration leaves the database at the previous version.
judgment: Money is a count of cents and the needs/wants/savings split uses the largest-remainder method, so the parts always add back to the income to the cent; a damaged backup is refused before anything is replaced.

name: llm-serving-eval-kit
question: Given a model and some GPUs, how many do you need, why did the server not start, and are two benchmark runs even comparable?
condition: differed between my RTX 4090 and A100 runs; the kit flags them instead of letting the comparison stand
